name: Economy
tag: What will AI do to growth, work, and production?
intro: Economy asks what happens when cognitive work becomes cheap: to growth and productivity, to jobs, wages, and careers, to firms and markets, to science and public services, and to how the gains and costs are distributed.

qs.q: Will AI modestly increase productivity, restore rapid twentieth-century-style growth, or produce historically unprecedented economic expansion?
qs.n: Acemoglu's task-based estimate is ~0.7% total TFP over a decade; Epoch-style growth models argue full automation implies growth rates without historical precedent. The disagreement is about substitution depth, not arithmetic.

links.t: Explosive Growth from AI: A Review of the Arguments
The Simple Macroeconomics of AI

qs.q: How long will organizations take to redesign processes, software, incentives, and management around AI?
qs.n: General-purpose technologies historically take decades to show up in productivity statistics, because value requires organizational reinvention. The J-curve predicts measured productivity dips before it surges. The live counter-argument is self-diffusion: unlike past general-purpose technologies, AI might do part of its own integration work — writing the code, redesigning the processes — compressing the historical lag.

links.t: The Productivity J-Curve
The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI

qs.q: How much value requires new infrastructure, data systems, robotics, training, and organizational change?
qs.n: The general-purpose-technology literature argues intangible investment — process redesign, data, retraining — historically dwarfs spending on the technology itself; whether AI follows that pattern or diffuses more cheaply is the open question.

links.t: AI Adoption and System-Wide Change

qs.q: Will AI mainly make existing goods cheaper, or create entirely new products, services, scientific projects, and consumer desires?
qs.n: Bessen's finding: automation raises employment where demand is elastic. Whether AI creates new wants — as electricity and computing did — or merely cheapens old ones largely decides the labor-market outcome.

links.t: AI and Jobs: The Role of Demand

qs.q: Even if cognitive work becomes cheap, will housing, energy, regulation, physical production, and institutional capacity limit growth?
qs.n: Baumol's cost disease, inverted: growth is set by the sectors AI can't accelerate, not the ones it can. The strongest skeptical case catalogues the physical, regulatory, and institutional drags that cheap cognition doesn't remove.

links.t: Why Transformative AI Is Really, Really Hard to Achieve
Artificial Intelligence and Economic Growth

qs.q: Which tasks and occupations will be automated, augmented, transformed, or newly created — and how quickly?
qs.n: Exposure studies flag most occupations as partially exposed; real usage data shows adoption concentrated in software, writing, and analysis. The augmentation-vs-automation split within tasks is the number to watch.
qs.crux: Will AI primarily complement human labor or substitute for it?

links.t: GPTs are GPTs: Labor Market Impact Potential of LLMs
The Anthropic Economic Index

qs.q: Could AI reduce worker bargaining power and wages even without producing large increases in unemployment?
qs.n: Acemoglu-Restrepo show 'so-so automation' can depress wages without mass unemployment. Autor's counter-case: AI could rebuild middle-skill work by extending expertise to more people. Both are live.

links.t: Tasks, Automation, and the Rise in US Wage Inequality
The Turing Trap
AI Could Actually Help Rebuild the Middle Class

qs.q: What happens if junior coding, analysis, research, design, legal, and administrative work disappears before senior roles?
qs.n: One prominent study finds relative employment declines for young workers in the most AI-exposed occupations since late 2022, concentrated where AI automates rather than augments; critics attribute the pattern to interest-rate and remote-work confounds.

links.t: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Employment Effects of AI
Looking for the Ladder

qs.q: How will people become experts if AI performs the apprenticeship tasks through which expertise was previously developed?
qs.n: Beane's 'shadow learning' research showed automation strips juniors of deliberate practice; generative AI compresses novice-expert performance gaps at work — while its effect on the practice through which expertise forms is the open question.

links.t: Learning to Work with Intelligent Machines
Generative AI at Work

qs.q: Can education, retraining, labor mobility, credentialing, and social insurance adapt quickly enough?
qs.n: Labor-market institutions adapt on decade timescales; AI capability moves faster. The policy inventory — retraining, wage insurance, credential reform — exists on paper and is largely untested at speed.

links.t: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: AI and the Labour Market
The Work of the Future

qs.q: Will profits accrue mainly to chipmakers, energy providers, cloud platforms, frontier labs, application companies, data owners, or AI-enabled incumbents?
qs.n: So far value has pooled in chips and cloud. Whether the model layer or the application layer captures more going forward — and whether revenue justifies the capex — is Sequoia's '$600B question.'

links.t: Who Owns the Generative AI Platform?
AI's $600B Question

qs.q: Will scale economies produce a few dominant firms, or will open models and falling inference costs commoditize intelligence?
qs.n: Scale economies, data feedback loops, and capital walls point to oligopoly; open weights and collapsing inference prices point to commodity. Competition authorities are watching the vertical stack, not just the model market.
qs.crux: Will capability remain concentrated in a few controllable institutions or proliferate widely?

links.t: Market Concentration Implications of Foundation Models
AI Foundation Models: Initial Report

qs.q: Will companies become smaller because coordination is cheap, or larger because AI rewards data, capital, distribution, and centralized control?
qs.n: Coase's transaction-cost logic cuts both ways: cheap coordination shrinks the reason firms exist, while data and capital advantages push toward giantism. The empirical race is on.

links.t: From Coase to AI Agents
The Coasean Singularity? Market Design with AI Agents

qs.q: What markets emerge when agents can search, negotiate, purchase, advertise, trade, and contract with one another?
qs.n: Agent-to-agent commerce raises market-design questions — identity, recourse, collusion, price formation — that economists are just beginning to formalize, and that infrastructure choices will lock in early.

links.t: Virtual Agent Economies
Virtual Agent Economies

qs.q: How should boards oversee systems participating in hiring, pricing, capital allocation, compliance, and strategy?
qs.n: Fiduciary duty when strategy is machine-advised is unsettled law and unsettled practice. Board oversight frameworks for AI are being drafted in real time, mostly by analogy to cyber risk.

links.t: The Artificially Intelligent Boardroom
links.s: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance

links.t: Board Oversight of AI
links.s: Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance

qs.q: In which fields will AI-driven discovery translate into real scientific and economic payoff — and how soon?
qs.n: Amodei's 'compressed 21st century' makes biology the test case for AI-driven conceptual breakthroughs; the skeptical view is that AI mostly accelerates the searchable parts of science. AlphaFold remains the clearest widely recognized example so far. (Whether AI can originate important ideas at all is treated under Trajectory 1.5.)

links.t: Machines of Loving Grace
A New Golden Age of Discovery: AI for Science

qs.q: How will science cope with a flood of plausible hypotheses, generated papers, synthetic data, and results that few humans can independently verify?
qs.n: Messeri & Crockett's warning: AI can produce more science while producing less understanding — epistemic monocultures where everyone's hypotheses come from the same models and nobody can check the volume.

links.t: AI and Illusions of Understanding in Scientific Research

qs.q: Why does demonstrated diagnostic capability keep outrunning delivered care — and can deployment close the gap without opaque errors and unequal access?
qs.n: Diagnostic parity keeps arriving in trials ahead of deployment, liability frameworks, and reimbursement; how much of the remaining gap is institutional rather than technical is the live dispute.

links.t: Towards Conversational Diagnostic Artificial Intelligence
Ethics and Governance of AI for Health: Guidance on Large Multi-Modal Models

qs.q: Who benefits if the scarce inputs are compute, intellectual property, electricity, data, and capital rather than human work?
qs.n: Korinek-Stiglitz: if AI substitutes broadly for labor, wages can fall even as output soars, and distribution then depends entirely on who owns the machines. Transition-scenario modeling makes the wage-collapse case precise.
qs.crux: Who will own the productive capital and infrastructure through which AI's gains flow?

links.t: AI and Its Implications for Income Distribution and Unemployment
Scenarios for the Transition to AGI

qs.q: Will developing countries gain access to cheap expertise, or lose the low-cost-labor development path that supported earlier industrialization?
qs.n: The IMF finds advanced economies more exposed but better positioned to benefit. The deeper worry: AI may pull up the export-led development ladder just as the largest-ever cohort of young workers reaches it.

links.t: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
A New Growth Strategy for Developing Nations

qs.q: Could broader capital ownership, sovereign funds, social dividends, UBI, negative income taxes, or shorter workweeks distribute gains effectively?
qs.n: Proposals range from Altman's taxed-equity 'Moore's Law for Everything' to windfall clauses committing labs to share extreme profits. The design question — mechanisms, not just transfers — is underdeveloped relative to its stakes.

links.t: Moore's Law for Everything
The Windfall Clause
The Employment Effects of a Guaranteed Income: Experimental Evidence from Two U.S. States

qs.q: Can electrical grids, water systems, land, and local communities accommodate rapidly growing compute demand?
qs.n: The IEA projects data-center electricity demand roughly doubling by 2030, with AI the main driver. Siting, water, and grid interconnection queues are where the abstraction meets local politics.

links.t: Energy and AI
AI's Power Requirements Under Exponential Growth

qs.q: Could synchronized agents, correlated models, concentrated investment, automated trading, or an AI-capex reversal create systemic risks?
qs.n: Regulators flag herding from correlated models, dependence on a few providers, and the sheer scale of AI capital expenditure as systemic scenarios — a financial-stability watchlist that barely existed two years ago.

links.t: The Financial Stability Implications of AI
Global Financial Stability Report, Ch. 3: AI and Capital Markets
